new_statements.translation: Tones. There are at least two, marked by the acute and grave accents: sẽéto 'mucus' and sẽèto 'honey', cèm 'potash' and cém 'blood', nõtɔ 'Bulba (person)' and nõtɔ 'farmer' differ by tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Prost treats Notre as a tone language with at least two lexically contrastive tones (acute = high, grave = low), illustrated by noun minimal pairs; he writes tones only where they distinguish words (cf. the noun-class list footnote 'Diffère par le ton du mot signifiant Bulba'). He makes no statement about word stress or an accent d'intensité; snippet-level searches of the whole sketch for 'accent', 'intensité', 'tonique', 'syllabe', 'hauteur', 'quantité' found no other passage, so the sketch appears silent on stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the tone inventory itself is hedged ('au moins deux').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: isolated nouns in citation form (minimal pairs); no phrase-level or verb tone discussion visible in the snippets.
new_statements.identity_note: Prost's sketch describes the speech of a single Bulba informant, Augustine Kiati (Intro, p. 629); he calls the language nõtre/bulba and notes it is 'très proche du mõore' (Western Oti-Volta), with a tradition of origin from the Koudougou area of Mossi country. Same variety as Glottolog notr1240 / ISO bly (Nootre, Boulba, Burusa); no dialects are distinguished in any source seen. Wikipedia files it under Moré-Dagbani; Glottolog under Oti-Volta.
